title: Absolute Convergence and Taylor Expansion in Web Based Models of Linear Logic
abstract:
We provide in this paper a generic construction of web models of linear logic with partial sums. Our construction captures a wide class of orthogonality models, ranging from coherence spaces to probabilistic coherence spaces, finiteness spaces and Köthe spaces. All these models are built on the same principles, but were very heterogeneous in the specificities of their technical development. Our construction factorizes these specificities, allowing a unified treatment of further developments, such as differentiation and Taylor expansion.
The differential λ-calculus relates quantitative aspects of programs to differentiation and to Taylor expansion in models of linear logic. Recent work has generalized the axioms of Taylor expansion, so that they apply to many models that only feature partial sums. However, that work did not cover Köthe spaces and finiteness spaces. We generalize the theory of Taylor expansion to models in which coefficients can be negative, and we prove that our generic web models always satisfy this new axiomatization. Therefore, all the aforementioned models feature a Taylor expansion.

Introduction
Quantitative semantics was introduced with linear logic after Girard noticed that the
interpretation of programs in mathematical models, were analytic maps [19]. They can be
written as an infinite sum of multilinear maps through a formula called the Taylor expansion:

The n-th derivative at 0 captures the part of the program that uses its input exactly n-times
during execution. In this way, quantitative semantics helps us understand how computation
interacts with non-determinism [33], probabilities [11, 15] or quantum primitives [41].
    The differential λ-calculus [16] and the syntactic Taylor expansion [17] extend quantitative
semantics. They give a purely syntactic way to track resources by building derivatives and
Taylor expansion inside the language itself. These theories also uncover a strong link between
the world of logic and computation, and the world of topology and analysis [12, 13, 26, 27].
    The differential λ-calculus [6] and the syntactical Taylor expansion, and their models [37]
have a fatal drawback: they allow any countable sums. The only way to interpret such sums
computationally is as non-determinism. From a syntactic viewpoint, this is puzzling. Indeed,

       Taylor expansion can be applied to deterministic [17] or probabilistic [10] programs, and enjoys
       uniformity properties that are needed to prove normalization [17, 46]. From a semantic
       viewpoint, allowing countable sums rules out most quantitative semantics. Fortunately,
       recent works show that the differential calculus [14, 18] and the Taylor expansion [18] can be
       axiomatized using only partial sums. Partial sums match computational behaviors such as
       determinism in coherence spaces [19], or randomness in probabilistic coherence spaces [11].
           One limitation remains. The infinite partial sums used in the coherent theory of Taylor
       expansion [18] rely on Σ-monoids [21]. Σ-monoids only allow positive sums: if x + y = 0 then
       x = y = 0. For programming language semantics, this is not a problem as programs never
       cancel each other out. However, this restriction becomes a serious issue when developing
       a theory of Taylor expansion that also works for quantitative semantics built on analysis
       and topology. In particular, Köthe spaces [12] and finiteness spaces [13] are important
       quantitative models that use analytic maps. Because they involve negative coefficients, they
       are not covered by the coherent Taylor expansion described in [18].

       Contributions. We develop in Part I a generic construction of web models of linear logic
       with partial sums. Our construction unifies results on web models that were very similar in
       ideas, but featured very heterogeneous technical details. We first consider models in which
       objects are sets of vectors and morphisms are matrices whose coefficients range over an
       arbitrary Σ-monoid. Then, we generalize our construction to a more general notion of partial
       sums called PCMs [22]. We consider here PCMs whose summability is given by a notion of
       absolute convergence. This describes web models in which coefficients can be negative, as in
       Köthe spaces [12] and finiteness spaces [13].
           In Part II, we generalize the coherent Taylor expansion of [18] to PCMs. This axiomatiz-
       ation of partial sum is more subtle to work with, in the same way that summability over real
       numbers is more subtle than summability over non-negative real numbers. We then prove in
       a unified way that all the web models developed in Part I feature such Taylor expansion.

       Related work. The use of partial sums in semantics is rather common, and can be traced
       back to algebraic programming semantics [36]. Various notions of positive sums have been
       used in the literature, such as in geometry of interaction [21] and quantum programming
       semantics [43, 7]. Our results on web models provide a unified point of view on various proof
       techniques that appear throughout the literature on web based semantics [19, 12, 13, 11, 33].
       Under some light additional assumptions (see Remark 32), our web models based on Σ-
       monoids can be described as categories of modules over Σ-semirings [45] with an orthogonal
       basis reminiscent of tight orthogonality in double glueing [23]. However, [45] does not describe
       Taylor expansion in that setting, and even though they prove that their model have a Lafont
       exponential, they do not provide any explicit definition. They also do not provide a definition
       for more general PCMs based on absolute convergence. Our theory of coherent Taylor
       expansion is an adaptation of the coherent Taylor expansion of [18] to a setting with possibly
       negative coefficients. Our work lies in the field of categorical differentiation, whose aim is to
       study the categorical properties of differentiation [2, 3, 8] and of Taylor expansion [25, 34, 47].

 8       Conclusion and future work

In Part I, we have built a generic construction of web models, based on strong and absolute
PCMs. It unifies various models of the literature. In Part II, we have described a theory
of Taylor expansion in categories enriched over PCMs. Web models given by our generic
construction feature such Taylor expansion as proved in Section 7. Thus, Taylor expansion is
compatible with the computational properties described by partial sums, such as determinism,
finite or countable non-determinism, randomness, and absolute convergence.


Future work. We conjecture that the exponential of our web models is always Lafont (see
Remark 25). Our theory of coherent Taylor expansion captures a wide class of web models,
but there are no known web-free examples. We conjecture that the analytic version [26] of
the category of convenient vector spaces [4] is not a representable PCM category but features
a coherent Taylor expansion. Finally, although we described our web models with a strong
emphasis on the algebraic point of view of partial sums, it should be possible to adopt a
topological viewpoint on absolute PCMs, as it is done in Köthe spaces [12] and finiteness
spaces [13].
